pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 1: A hat is only a hat until it is a goose.*

Marnie Pennywhistle was expelled from Humbleton Academy of Practical Wizardry at fourteen minutes past nine on a Tuesday morning, which she thought was rude of them, because she hadn't even had breakfast.

To be fair, there was a goose involved.

The goose was sitting on the Principal's desk. He was a plump white goose with an orange beak and a purple ribbon around his neck, spangled with silver stars, and he was honking at a paperweight as if it owed him money. Around him the Principal's office went on being as stately as ever. The portraits on the walls tutted whenever anybody sneezed. A clock ticked in the careful way of a clock that has never once been late. And on every shelf sat a hat, because Humbleton collected hats the way other schools collect trophies.

Marnie stood in the middle of the carpet in her forest-green cloak, with her copper-red hair coming out of its two buns and a pencil sticking out of one of them, and tried to look like a person who could not possibly have done it.
pages.image: A stately wizard school Principal's office with portraits on the walls and shelves full of tall hats; on the big desk Gerald with an orange beak and a purple ribbon with silver stars around his neck honks at a paperweight, while in the middle of the carpet Marnie, an eleven-year-old girl with freckles and wild copper-red hair in two puffy buns with a pencil stuck in one, in a forest-green cloak with a crooked silver clasp, mustard cardigan and red high-top sneakers, tries to look innocent.

pages.text:
It had happened ten minutes earlier, at the Founders' Day rehearsal in the Great Hall.

The whole school had been standing in rows, the choir had been warming up, and Principal Thistlewood had been giving a speech about precision. He wore his tall purple hat with the silver stars, as he had every day for forty years. And the hat, as Marnie noticed halfway through the second paragraph, was crooked.

It was crooked by about the width of a thumb. It was the sort of crooked that gets under your skin like a splinter. Marnie knew she should leave it alone. She knew it the way you know you shouldn't poke a sleeping bear. But the hat tilted, and tilted, and the Principal said the word "perfect" for the ninth time, and her wand was already in her hand.

"Straighten," she whispered. It was only the smallest spell in the book.

There was a puff of purple smoke. The hat went *hoo*, and then it went *honk*.

The goose flew once round the Great Hall at roof height. It knocked over the entire choir, bit the Vice-Principal on the toe, and landed in the punch.
pages.image: The Great Hall of a wizard school in uproar: Gerald with a purple starred ribbon flaps above rows of toppled choir children while a tall thin old Principal with a long curled white moustache and a purple robe stares upward with his hair standing on end; a tiny Marnie with copper-red hair buns and a wand stands frozen at the back, and a bowl of pink punch splashes up below.

pages.text:
Now Principal Ambrose Thistlewood sat behind his desk, tall and thin, with a long white moustache curled up at the ends like two question marks, and read out the charges from a very long piece of paper.

"One goose," he said. "Fourteen pecked toes. Three flattened choirs. One punch bowl, which was a gift from the Ministry. One Vice-Principal, who is now in the infirmary, being brave."

By the door stood a boy in a crisp royal-blue blazer with gold buttons. His name was Cassius Pomeroy, he was the head of the Golden Circle, which was what Humbleton called its very best students, and his golden hair was perfect. It was perfect in the Great Hall and perfect on the stairs and, as far as anyone could tell, perfect in a hurricane. He was not laughing. That was the worst of it. He wore the smile of a freshly ironed shirt.

"Perfectly sad, really," he murmured, to nobody, but loudly enough.
pages.image: The Principal's office: Principal Thistlewood, a tall thin old man with a long curled white moustache and a purple robe with silver stars, sits behind his desk reading from a very long scroll that unrolls onto the floor, while in the doorway Cassius, a twelve-year-old boy with perfect slicked golden hair, a crisp royal-blue blazer with gold buttons and shiny black shoes, stands with a neat smile, and Marnie in her green cloak shrinks in the middle of the carpet, with Gerald nearby.

pages.text:
Marnie knew the list by heart. She had been at Humbleton for two years, and in that time her candle spell had made a fish, her levitation spell had made Professor Dunmore's moustache stand straight up, and her Tidy spell had turned the dust bunnies under her bed into rabbits, real ones, with real opinions.

It was never the spell in the book. It was always something close to it, in the way that a cousin is close to you, but wearing a different hat.

"It appears," the Principal said, "that the goose is permanent. Which is highly irregular." His moustache twitched. "Miss Pennywhistle, some people are simply not suited to magic. It is no shame. But it is a fact."

"I'm sorry," said Marnie. And she was. She was sorrier than she had ever been about anything. But sorry, it turned out, doesn't fit back into a goose.

The Principal folded the long paper into a very small square, and the clock ticked, and the portraits tutted, and Marnie understood that she had not been sent home for a day or for a week. She had been sent home for good.
pages.image: Close on Marnie, an eleven-year-old girl with freckles and wild copper-red hair in two puffy buns with a pencil stuck in one, in a forest-green cloak, looking down sadly with her hands clasped, while behind her on the desk Gerald with a purple starred ribbon tilts his head, and a portrait on the wall seems to tut; soft sorrowful lamplight.

pages.text:
She left the way people leave when they are not allowed to come back: slowly, with her trunk.

The trunk had a wheel that squeaked at every second step. The goose followed her down the corridor, because nobody else in the entire school wanted him and he seemed to have decided, in his goosey way, that she would do. At the great front doors, Cassius appeared at her elbow without making a sound.

"Goodbye, Pennywhistle," he said. "Do try to stay… correct."

The big doors boomed shut behind her.

Marnie stood on the top step in the cold morning, with her trunk and her cloak and a goose, and no school. The goose turned and honked at the doors, long and loud and deeply offended, as if to say that Humbleton could do with a few more geese, and fewer hats.

And Marnie laughed. It was a small, wet laugh, and it surprised her very much.

She did not know it yet, but it was the best thing that would ever happen to her. It was only the beginning, and it had feathers.
pages.image: Marnie, an eleven-year-old girl with freckles and wild copper-red hair in two puffy buns with a pencil stuck in one, in a forest-green cloak and red high-top sneakers, stands on the top step of a stately golden-stone school entrance with a small trunk on a squeaky wheel, laughing through tears, while Gerald with a purple starred ribbon honks angrily back at the closed front doors; morning light.
